title: My Life Without Me
full_review:
A young wife and mother examines her life in the face of death in the three-hankie tearjerker "My Life Without Me" (Sony Classics).

Death is never an easy issue to deal with, especially when it comes to the death of a young person who will also leave behind a husband and two young daughters. Such is the premise of writer-director Isabel Coixet's unflinching and heartbreaking story about 23-year-old Ann (Sarah Polley), who -- after mistakenly believing she is suffering from anemia -- is diagnosed with terminal cancer which leaves her only a couple of months to live.

Instead of sinking into a pool of self-pity, Ann decides to take action, making a list of all the things she wants to do before dying, including recording birthday tapes for her two young daughters Penny (Jessica Amlee) and Patsy (Kanya Jo Kennedy) and visiting her estranged father (Alfred Molina) in prison. She also chooses not to tell anyone, which means keeping husband Don (Scott Speedman) and her mother (Deborah Harry) in the dark.

Ann begins an affair with Lee (Mark Ruffalo), the handsome and emotionally scarred stranger she meets at the coin laundry, who demands nothing of her except to let him love her.

Apparently tissues were handed out at the New York City premiere, and with good cause. Although the film is predictable in the sense that viewers know Ann will die, it is more about what she does with the time she has left. Her death is a nonevent. The movie's strength is that it does not revert to mawkish sentimentality or turn into a disease-of-the-week telefilm. However, watching working-class Ann try to continue on with her life in her tiny trailer park, kissing her girls' foreheads or making them special pancakes, is nonetheless a dismal experience.

This is part of the problem with the film. As Ann grapples with her imminent death, the film becomes more and more morose, leaving the viewer drained as the sadness of the situation becomes unbearable. Rarely is one relieved of this misery by some uplifting sentiment. It also makes one reflect on how dismal the prospect of death is in the absence of faith. For Ann, there is just blackness after life is over. And while death is almost always difficult, Catholic faith in eternal life offers some comfort in the face of such pain. It is also a reminder to live each day to the fullest.

Depressing yet uncompromising, "My Life Without Me," which was executive produced by Pedro Almodovar, will leave one sapped, but will give one much to think about as well.

Because of an extramarital affair and sporadic rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
